name: FaceMaster

lead: FaceMaster is a consumer device that stimulates facial muscles with electrical pulses delivered through two handheld probes with foam pads. The aim is firmer, more toned and lifted-looking facial contours.

The US FDA cleared it in 2005 for cosmetic facial stimulation. A randomized trial of a comparable facial neuromuscular stimulation device found thicker cheek muscle and self-reported improvements in firmness and lift after 12 weeks; that trial did not test FaceMaster itself.

paras: Users run on-device cycles (eye, facial and feathering) with the pads soaked in conductive solution, following the device's prompts, usually a few times a week. Manufacturer instructions note that lowering intensity can reduce sensations, and some users see flashing lights during use.

Clearance is for cosmetic use only, not medical treatment. A consumer blog reports that use on the neck may cause low blood pressure and fainting. Reviews are mixed, with some users reporting visible results and others finding claims overstated.

angle.text: The device exercises facial muscles by electrical stimulation, with the aim of giving fuller, firmer-looking cheeks and a lifted appearance. Users apply it in short sessions several times a week.

lead: FaceMaster is a home facial toning system made by FaceMaster of Beverly Hills, Inc. It uses a control module and two handheld probes with foam pads soaked in a conductive solution to deliver low-level electrical stimulation to facial muscles [1]. It is promoted as a way to firm and lift the face.

The FDA cleared the device on June 1, 2005, through the 510(k) route, citing the Rejuvenique Facial Toning System as its predicate. It is classed as a transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulator for cosmetic facial muscle toning, indicated for over-the-counter use [1]. Actress Suzanne Somers was associated with its US marketing.

Published research examines facial neuromuscular electrical stimulation in general. A 2012 randomized trial of one such device in 108 women reported increased cheek-muscle thickness and improved self-rated firmness [2].
infobox: Control module, two handheld probes with foam pads

paras: The system consists of a control module and two handheld probes with foam pads that are soaked in conductive solution. Users follow prompts through three cycles named eye, facial and feathering [1].

FaceMaster of Beverly Hills, Inc. of Calabasas, California received 510(k) clearance for the device on June 1, 2005. The clearance is for cosmetic stimulation of the face for over-the-counter home use [1].

No studies found of FaceMaster itself. A related randomized, partially blinded trial of a different facial neuromuscular electrical stimulation device enrolled 108 healthy women (mean age 43.7). Twelve weeks of 20-minute sessions five days a week was associated with an 18.6% increase in zygomatic major muscle thickness, and at least 80% of users reported improved firmness, tone and lift versus under 5% of controls [2].

The manufacturer's instructions state that lowering intensity can reduce sensations and that flashing lights may occur [3]. A consumer blog reports that using it on the neck can lower blood pressure and cause fainting. Retail reviews are mixed.
